title: Equivalence & the Laws
goal: Decide whether two formulas are equivalent: prove it with a chain of named laws, or disprove it with one row.
magic: `≡` = identical truth-table columns. One differing row disproves it.
Implication: `p ⇒ q ≡ ¬p ∨ q`. De Morgan flips `∧ ↔ ∨` as `¬` goes in.
Chain proofs: remove arrows → push `¬` in → distribute/factor → tidy. One named law per line.
Substitute into a tautology everywhere → still a tautology. Swap in an equivalent piece → still equivalent.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
`≡`: same truth value in every row
blocks.summary: Two formulas are equivalent when their truth-table columns are identical. One differing row disproves it.
blocks.picture: Two different recipes that always produce the same cake. You can swap one recipe for the other and nobody can tell. Equivalent formulas are like that, and that's how circuit designers swap a big circuit for a smaller one.
blocks.official: `φ ≡ ψ` (**logically equivalent**) if they have the same truth value for **all** values of their basic propositions (Week 2, slide 10). Equivalent formulas give digital circuits that compute the same function, so equivalences are used to **optimise circuits**. To **disprove** an equivalence, **one** row where the two sides differ is enough (slide 13).

steps: Try to find a row where they differ.
watch.answer: **Not equivalent.** Counterexample row `p = T, q = F`. (The correct De Morgan is `¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q`.)

tries.q: Is `¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q`? If not, give a row where they differ.
tries.a: **No.** Row `p = T, q = F`: left `¬(T)` = F, right `F ∨ T` = T.
tries.why: De Morgan flips `∨` to `∧`: `¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q`.
Both are false only in the row `p = T, q = F` (it's the contrapositive).

tries.q: Is `p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ r`? If not, a row.
tries.a: **No.** Row `p = T, r = F` (any `q`): left T, right F.
tries.why: Moving brackets around a mix of `∨` and `∧` changes the meaning. The real law distributes `p ∨` into **both** parts.

tries.q: `φ ≡ ψ`. Which formula is then valid?
tries.why: `φ ≡ ψ` exactly when `⊨ φ ⇔ ψ` (Week 2, slide 27).

trap.tempting: They agree in the rows I tried, so they're equivalent.
trap.correct: Equivalent needs **every** row. A few matching rows prove nothing; one differing row disproves it.
trap.test: To prove `≡`: a full table or a chain of laws. To disprove: one row.

blocks.magic: `≡` = identical columns. One different row = not equivalent.

blocks.title: The law toolkit
blocks.summary: Twelve named laws. Each one lets you swap one shape for another without changing the meaning.
blocks.picture: Like algebra rules you already trust: `a + b = b + a`, `a(b + c) = ab + ac`. Logic has its own list, and every step of an equivalence proof must name one.
blocks.official: The lecture's list (Week 2, slides 10–11) is in the table below. Two you'll use constantly: **Implication** `p ⇒ q ≡ ¬p ∨ q` (turns every arrow into `∨`), and **De Morgan** (pushes `¬` inside a bracket and flips `∧ ↔ ∨`).

watch.q: Name the law used in each step: `¬(¬p ∨ q)` → `¬¬p ∧ ¬q` → `p ∧ ¬q`.
steps: Step 1 pushes `¬` into a bracket and turns `∨` into `∧`: **De Morgan**.
watch.answer: De Morgan, then Double negation. So `¬(¬p ∨ q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q`, which is also `¬(p ⇒ q)`.

tries.why: A statement or its opposite: one of them is always true.

tries.q: Which law turns `(x ∧ y) ∨ (x ∧ z)` into `x ∧ (y ∨ z)`?
tries.why: `p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)`, read backwards.

tries.a: **Domination** (the slides list `p ∧ ⊥ ≡ ⊥` in the Identity group).
tries.why: An `∧` with a guaranteed-false part is false.
The Implication law's second line.
`¬(A ∧ B) ≡ ¬A ∨ ¬B` with `A = s`, `B = ¬t`, then double negation on `¬¬t`.

trap.tempting: De Morgan just puts `¬` on each letter: `¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q`.
trap.correct: De Morgan **also flips the joiner**: `¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q`.
trap.test: Test with `p = T, q = F`: "not both" is true, "neither" is false.

blocks.magic: `⇒` becomes `¬A ∨ B`. `¬` goes inside by flipping `∧ ↔ ∨`.

blocks.title: Proving `≡` with a chain of laws
blocks.summary: Start from one side, change one thing per line, and name the law each time until you reach the other side.
blocks.picture: Like refactoring code: each commit makes one small safe change, and you note which rule made it safe. The last version behaves exactly like the first.
blocks.official: Write `φ ≡ … ≡ ψ` with **one law per step**, named on the right (Week 2, slide 12 does this for a four-step chain ending in `¬p ∨ q`; slide 14 proves `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ (p ⇒ r) ≡ p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)` this way). The usual plan: (1) remove `⇒` and `⇔`, (2) push `¬` inward with De Morgan, (3) distribute or factor, (4) clean up with Excluded middle / Identity / Domination.

watch.answer: Done in three named steps. In words: "if `p` then `q`, and if `p` then `r`" = "if `p` then both".

tries.q: Prove `p ∨ (¬p ∧ q) ≡ p ∨ q`. (This is the lecture's program-logic example, Week 1 slide 56.)
tries.a: `p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)` `≡ (p ∨ ¬p) ∧ (p ∨ q)` (Distribution) `≡ ⊤ ∧ (p ∨ q)` (Excluded middle) `≡ p ∨ q` (Identity).
tries.why: So `if x > 0 or (x <= 0 and y > 100)` can be simplified to `if x > 0 or y > 100`.
Factor out the common `a`, and the rest becomes `⊤`.

tries.a: `(p ∨ q) ⇒ r` `≡ ¬(p ∨ q) ∨ r` (Implication) `≡ (¬p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r` (De Morgan) `≡ (¬p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r)` (Distribution) `≡ (p ⇒ r) ∧ (q ⇒ r)` (Implication).
tries.why: "If either one, then `r`" = "each one alone leads to `r`".

tries.q: Simplify `¬(p ⇒ ¬q)` as far as possible, naming each law.
tries.why: "It's not the case that `p` rules out `q`" means both happen.

trap.tempting: Do three changes in one line to save time.
trap.correct: One law per line, named. Markers give credit for each justified step, and big jumps hide mistakes.
trap.test: Read each line: can you name exactly one law that got you here?

blocks.magic: Remove arrows → push `¬` in → distribute/factor → tidy up. Name every step.

blocks.title: Disproving: find the one row where they differ
blocks.summary: Don't build two full tables: aim straight for a row that makes one side T and the other F.
blocks.picture: A spot-the-difference puzzle: you don't need to list everything that matches. One difference is enough to say the pictures aren't the same.
blocks.official: To show `φ ≢ ψ`, give **one** assignment where they differ (Week 2, slide 13: `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ r` vs `p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)` differ at `p = F, q = T, r = F`). **Trick:** make the side with an `⇒` false on purpose (left T, right F), then check the other side.

steps: Try the simplest row, `p = F, q = F`.
Left: `p ⇔ q` = T, so `¬(p ⇔ q)` = F.
watch.answer: **Not equivalent** (row `p = F, q = F`). In fact `¬p ⇔ ¬q ≡ p ⇔ q`: negating **both** sides of `⇔` changes nothing.

tries.q: Is `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ r ≡ (p ∧ q) ⇒ r`? If not, a row.
tries.a: **No.** Row `p = F, q = F, r = F`: left (T ⇒ F) = F, right (F ⇒ F) = T.
tries.why: Make the left false: its left side `p ⇒ q` must be T and `r` = F. `p = F` does that. Then the right side has a false condition, so it's T.
Both sides become `¬p ∨ q ∨ r` after the Implication law (and Idempotence for the duplicated `¬p`).
tries.wrong: If you went looking for a counterexample and found none: that's the sign it's true. Prove it with the chain instead.

tries.why: Left: `¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r`. Right: `¬p ∨ r ∨ ¬q ∨ r`, which is the same after Idempotence.
When `p` = F both sides are T. When `p` = T both sides reduce to `q ⇔ r`.

trap.tempting: Two formulas that look different must be different.
trap.correct: Look-alikes can differ and different-looking ones can match. Only rows (or laws) decide.
trap.test: Before hunting for a counterexample, spend 20 seconds rewriting both sides with the Implication law.

blocks.magic: One differing row disproves `≡`. No row found? Prove it with laws.

blocks.title: Two substitution rules
blocks.summary: Replace a letter everywhere in a tautology → still a tautology. Replace a piece by an equivalent piece → still equivalent.
blocks.picture: A spell that works for *any* ingredient keeps working if you plug in a whole potion instead of one ingredient. And swapping an ingredient for an identical one never changes the result.
blocks.official: **Rule 1** (Week 2, slide 40): if `⊨ φ(P)`, then `⊨ φ(α)`, where `α` replaces **every** occurrence of the letter `P`. Example: `⊨ P ⇒ (P ∨ Q)`, so `⊨ (A ∨ B) ⇒ (A ∨ B ∨ Q)`. **Rule 2** (slide 41): if `α ≡ β`, replacing an occurrence of `α` inside `φ` by `β` gives an equivalent formula. Example: `P ⇒ Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q`, so `Q ⇒ (P ⇒ Q) ≡ Q ⇒ (¬P ∨ Q)`.

watch.q: `⊨ (P ∧ Q) ⇒ P`. Substitute `x ⇒ y` for `P`. What do you get, and is it valid?
steps: Rule 1 says a tautology stays a tautology.
watch.answer: **`((x ⇒ y) ∧ Q) ⇒ (x ⇒ y)`**, valid by substitution. No truth table needed.

tries.why: Every `P` gets `(a ∨ b)`, with brackets.

tries.q: You substitute `r` for **only one** of the two `P`s in `P ⇒ P`, getting `r ⇒ P`. Is the result guaranteed valid?
tries.a: **No.** `r ⇒ P` is false at `r = T, P = F`.
tries.why: Rule 1 needs **every** occurrence replaced.

tries.q: Use Rule 2 and `¬(a ∧ b) ≡ ¬a ∨ ¬b` to rewrite `c ∨ ¬(a ∧ b)`.
tries.why: Swap the equivalent piece; the rest stays.

trap.tempting: Substitute into any formula and keep its truth value.
trap.correct: Rule 1 is for **tautologies**, and every occurrence must be replaced. Rule 2 needs the swapped piece to be **equivalent**.
trap.test: Ask: is the formula I'm substituting into valid? Did I replace every copy?

blocks.magic: Tautology + substitute everywhere = tautology. Swap in an equivalent piece = equivalent.

blocks.title: Exclusive or `⊕`: exactly one
blocks.summary: `p ⊕ q` is T when exactly one of them is T. It's the opposite of `⇔`.
blocks.picture: A hotel breakfast: "eggs or pancakes", meaning one or the other but not both. Or a two-way light switch: flip either switch and the light changes.
blocks.official: `A ⊕ B` (**exclusive or**, xor) is T exactly when `A` and `B` have **different** values (the Problem set 2 hint gives its table; it's the logic behind the set operation `⊕` from Week 1, slide 27). Useful facts: `p ⊕ q ≡ (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (¬p ∧ q) ≡ ¬(p ⇔ q) ≡ ¬p ⇔ q`, `p ⊕ ⊥ ≡ p`, `p ⊕ ⊤ ≡ ¬p`, `p ⊕ p ≡ ⊥`, `p ⊕ q ≡ q ⊕ p`.

steps: Row `p = F`: F ⊕ T = T (they differ), and `¬p` = T. ✅
Row `p = T`: T ⊕ T = F (they match), and `¬p` = F. ✅
watch.answer: Same column, so `p ⊕ ⊤ ≡ ¬p`: xor with true **flips** the bit (like `x ^ 1` in code).

tries.why: The sides differ.
"At least one, but not both" = exactly one.

tries.q: Is `a ⊕ b ≡ a ∨ b`? If not, a row.
tries.a: **No.** Row `a = T, b = T`: `⊕` gives F, `∨` gives T.
tries.why: "or" in logic is inclusive. `⊕` excludes the both-true row.
If `p` = F both sides are F. If `p` = T both sides are `q ⊕ r`.

trap.tempting: "or" in a logic formula means "one or the other, not both".
trap.correct: `∨` is **inclusive** (both is fine). Only `⊕` excludes both.
trap.test: Check the row where both are T: `∨` gives T, `⊕` gives F.

items.why: Saying the same thing twice adds nothing.
"Not (a or b)" = "neither".
Implication law.
Domination: an `∨` with a true part is true.
Double negation removes one pair of `¬`.
Order doesn't matter for `∨`.
Factor out the common `p ∨`.
De Morgan, then double negation on `¬¬a`. Also `= b ⇒ a`.
`≡ (¬s ∨ t) ∧ (¬s ∨ ¬t)` `≡ ¬s ∨ (t ∧ ¬t)` `≡ ¬s ∨ ⊥` `≡ ¬s`. If `s` led to both `t` and `¬t`, `s` must be false.
`≡ ¬m ∨ ¬m` (Implication) `≡ ¬m` (Idempotence).
`⇔` is T exactly when both are T or both are F.
`⊕` is T exactly when `⇔` is F.

blocks.sub: Problem set 2, Q4 style: *prove or disprove*. All pairs here are original.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `(p ∧ q) ∨ r ≡ p ∧ (q ∨ r)`.
items.a: **Disprove.** Row `p = F, q = F, r = T`: left F ∨ T = T, right F ∧ … = F.
items.why: The right side needs `p`; the left doesn't when `r` is true. Bracket position matters when `∧` and `∨` mix.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `p ∨ (q ⇔ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ⇔ (p ∨ r)`.
items.a: **Prove.** Case `p` = T: both sides are T (left by `∨`; right is T ⇔ T). Case `p` = F: both sides are `q ⇔ r` (Identity: `F ∨ x ≡ x`).
items.why: When a law list doesn't give a quick chain, a two-case argument on one letter is a valid proof.
De Morgan works for any number of parts: apply it twice.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `(p ⊕ q) ∧ r ≡ (p ∧ r) ⊕ q`.
items.a: **Disprove.** Row `p = F, q = T, r = F`: left (T) ∧ F = F, right F ⊕ T = T.
items.why: Set `r = F` to kill the left side, then make the right side T with `q = T`.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ p ≡ p`.
items.a: **Prove.** `≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q) ∨ p` (Implication, twice) `≡ (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ p` (De Morgan, Double negation) `≡ (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (p ∧ ⊤)` (Identity) `≡ p ∧ (¬q ∨ ⊤)` (Distribution) `≡ p ∧ ⊤` (Domination) `≡ p` (Identity).
items.why: Surprising but true (it's called Peirce's law). The last four steps are the *absorption* shortcut `p ∨ (p ∧ x) ≡ p`.

items.a: **Prove.** Contrapositive: `¬p ⇒ (q ∨ r) ≡ ¬(q ∨ r) ⇒ ¬¬p` `≡ (¬q ∧ ¬r) ⇒ p` (De Morgan, Double negation).
items.why: Swap-and-flip keeps the meaning; then tidy with De Morgan.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `(p ⇒ q) ∧ r ≡ p ⇒ (q ∧ r)`.
items.a: **Disprove.** Row `p = F, q = F, r = F`: left T ∧ F = F, right F ⇒ … = T.
items.why: The left side always needs `r`. The right only needs it when `p` holds.

items.q: A circuit computes `(x ∧ y) ∨ (¬x ∧ y) ∨ (x ∧ ¬y)`. Find the shortest equivalent formula, naming each law.
items.a: **`x ∨ y`.** `(x ∧ y) ∨ (¬x ∧ y) ≡ (x ∨ ¬x) ∧ y ≡ ⊤ ∧ y ≡ y` (Distribution, Excluded middle, Identity). Then `y ∨ (x ∧ ¬y) ≡ (y ∨ x) ∧ (y ∨ ¬y) ≡ (y ∨ x) ∧ ⊤ ≡ x ∨ y` (Distribution, Excluded middle, Identity, Commutativity).
items.why: Three gates' worth of logic shrink to one OR gate.

items.a: **`¬p ∧ ¬q`.** `¬(q ⇒ p) ≡ q ∧ ¬p`. So inside: `p ∨ (q ∧ ¬p) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬p) ≡ p ∨ q`. Then `¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q` (De Morgan).
items.why: Simplify the inside first; negate at the end.

items.q: Prove or disprove: `(p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ r) ∧ (r ⇒ p) ≡ (p ⇔ q) ∧ (q ⇔ r)`.
items.a: **Prove.** Both sides say that `p`, `q`, `r` all have the same value. Left: if any one is T, the cycle forces the next, so all are T; if any one is F, going backwards forces all F. Right: `p = q` and `q = r`.
items.why: A cycle of implications is as strong as all the `⇔`s.

items.q: Which options are equivalent to `¬(p ⇒ (q ∨ r))`?
items.why: `¬(p ⇒ X) ≡ p ∧ ¬X`, so the target is `p ∧ ¬(q ∨ r) ≡ p ∧ ¬q ∧ ¬r`. (5) is `(p ∧ ¬q) ∧ ¬r`. (2) is the un-negated formula. (4) allows `p = F`.

items.q: True or false: if `φ ≡ ψ`, then `¬φ ≡ ¬ψ`.
items.why: Identical columns stay identical when both are flipped. (It's also Rule 2 with the context `¬(…)`.)

items.a: `¬(p ∧ q) ⇒ r` `≡ (¬p ∨ ¬q) ⇒ r` (De Morgan, inside) `≡ ¬(¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ r` (Implication) `≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ r` (De Morgan, Double negation) `≡ (p ∨ r) ∧ (q ∨ r)` (Distribution) `≡ (¬p ⇒ r) ∧ (¬q ⇒ r)` (Implication, Double negation).
items.why: If not both, then `r`: missing `p` gives `r`, and missing `q` gives `r`.

items.q: Is `p ⇒ q ≡ q ⇒ p`? If not, a row.
items.a: **No.** Row `p = T, q = F` (or `p = F, q = T`).

lines: `φ ≡ ψ` ⇔ same value in every row ⇔ `⊨ φ ⇔ ψ`.
Disprove: one row. Prove: full table, a two-case split on one letter, or a chain of named laws.
Most-used laws: Implication, De Morgan, Double negation, Distribution, Excluded middle, Identity/Domination.
Substitution: every occurrence, into a tautology. Replacement: an equivalent piece.
`⊕`: exactly one is true. `p ⊕ ⊤ ≡ ¬p`, `p ⊕ ⊥ ≡ p`, `p ⊕ p ≡ ⊥`.
